# Brahmāyu Sutta (MN 91 (PTS MN ii 133))

**ID:** MN 91 (PTS MN ii 133)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Brahmāyu Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Brahmāyu
**PTS:** MN ii 133
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn91
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Brahmāyu Sutta* (MN 91; PTS MN ii 133) is the ninety-first discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, located in the Brāhmaṇavagga ("Chapter on Brahmins") [Anālayo 2017a; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The narrative centers on Brahmāyu, a venerable, 120-year-old brahmin scholar versed in the Vedic marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisa*), who sends his senior student Uttara to ascertain whether the ascetic Gotama truly possesses these thirty-two bodily characteristics [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2017a; Holt et al. 2003; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Uttara shadows the Buddha closely for several months, meticulously observing his daily comportment—how he walks, wears his robes, washes, sits, eats, and teaches [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2016; Anālayo 2017b]. While thirty marks are readily evident to Uttara, the Buddha must miraculously display his hidden genitals and extend his tongue to touch his ears and forehead to dispel any remaining doubt [Holt et al. 2003; Anālayo 2017b]. Persuaded by Uttara's report, Brahmāyu visits the Buddha in person, offers hospitality, receives the teaching, and attains non-returning (with the commentary noting the realization associated with the arising of the Dhamma eye) [SuttaCentral; Anderson 2013; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995].

The text is preserved in multiple early Buddhist recensions: full parallels exist in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 161 in T 26, associated with the Sarvāstivāda), an early independent Chinese translation attributed to Zhi Qian titled *Fanmoyu jing* (梵摩渝經, T 76), and Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SHT sutta53) [SuttaCentral; Anālayo 2017a; Nattier 2004]. Zhi Qian's translation contains distinctive interpretive glosses adapted for a Chinese audience and unique references to the twelve divisions of scriptures [Sen 2014; Nattier 2004], while the Madhyama-āgama version adds a concluding meal verse absent in the Pāli text [Shinohara 2010]. Descriptions of the thirty-two marks and Vedic interlocutors closely parallel discourses such as the *Mahāpadāna Sutta* (DN 14), *Ambaṭṭha Sutta* (DN 3), and *Sela Sutta* (MN 92 / Snp 3.7) [SuttaCentral; Holt et al. 2003]. DharmaNexus corroborates these cross-canonical links, identifying massive Pali-internal passage reuse with DN 3, the Vinaya *Khandhakas* (Kd 1 and Kd 6), MN 92, and *Aṅguttaranikāya* sets, as well as cross-language alignments with MĀ 161, the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, and Tibetan *Vinayavastu* traditions [DharmaNexus].

- Resembling parallels (SuttaCentral): DN 19 (PTS DN ii 220) Mahāgovinda Sutta; G-Dhp 1–50 Brammaṇavagga; Thig 4.1 Bhaddākāpilānītherīgāthā
